osmTags.inscription: This stone has been set in this place to commemorate the fusion of the English and Norman peoples which resulted from the great battle fought here in 1066

Diex Aie! Dans le champ historique de Senlac, où tomba le brave Harold le Saxon,837ans aprés la batallle qui donna a la Grande Bretagne la Loi Normande. Le Souvenir Normand venu des bord de la Seine a proclamé avec joie Ia Paix des Normandies Soeurs...

MCMXLVII
The old wall of the churchyard stood 8'3" in front of this stone
The area of the churchyard ceded to the highway was 184 sq yards

The traditional site of the High Altar of Battle Abbey
Founded to commemorate the victory of Duke William on 14 October 1066
The High Altar was placed to mark the spot where King Harold died

Reredorter
This reredorter or latrine was built in the mid 13th century. Monks had direct access to it from the dormitory. The paved main drain discharged down the valley: the large arches gave easy access for cleaning.
Since 1367 AD when Jocé a Smith or Ferror had a blacksmiths shop on or near this spot, an ironmonger has traded here. The present business started 1680 AD is probably the oldest in the British Isles
16th century two storey house, third floor added about 1700 AD. Langton House named after Elizabeth Langton, who endowed the local school

eras.label: Mapped site · auto T1
eras.summary: Mapped outline, terrain and present-day surroundings from open data. No historic reconstruction.
eras.basis: Everything drawn is traced from OpenStreetMap ways (ODbL) and the Terrarium elevation tiles. Each element names its OSM way.
eras.conjecture: Walls and buildings without a sourced height are drawn as kerb-high plan lines, never as masses. Closed walls have no gates: none are mapped. The DEM is ~30 m source resolution: it cannot show terraces, ditches or scarps. Nothing historic is depicted.
